slides.heading: Depreciation: spreading the cost of an asset
slides.body_md: Part 1: **depreciation**: meaning, causes, need, and the **straight line** and **written down value** methods.

nodes.label: It is used over its life
Part of its cost is charged each year
Profit and book value show the charge

visual.alt: Flow: an asset is bought at cost, used over its life, part of its cost is charged each year as depreciation, and profit and book value show the charge
visual.caption: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset over its life.

slides.narration: A business buys a machine once, but the machine helps earn revenue for many years. Depreciation spreads the cost of the machine over those years, so that each year bears its fair share. In this part we learn what depreciation is, why it arises, and how it is calculated by two methods. We work with imagined firms such as Rana Engineering and Sunder Tools.

slides.heading: What is depreciation?

rows: The book value of a fixed asset, through use, the passage of time or obsolescence
The depreciable cost of the asset is spread over its useful life
Against the revenue of each year, as an expense
It is not a payment of cash and not a measure of the market value

visual.alt: Table: what falls, what is done, where depreciation is charged and what it is not

slides.narration: Depreciation is the decline in the book value of a fixed asset because of use, the passage of time or obsolescence. In accounting it is the spreading of the depreciable cost of the asset over its useful life. It is charged against revenue as an expense each year. It is not a payment of cash, and it is not an attempt to find the market value of the asset.

slides.heading: Features of depreciation

rows: Each year the book value of the asset becomes lower
Machines, furniture and vehicles are depreciated; stock and debtors are not
The cash was paid when the asset was bought; no cash leaves when depreciation is charged
It is debited to the profit and loss account, so it reduces the profit of the year

visual.alt: Table of four features of depreciation

slides.narration: Depreciation has four features. First, it is a decline in the book value of the asset. Second, it applies to fixed assets, such as machines and furniture, and not to stock or debtors. Third, it is a non cash expense, because the cash was paid when the asset was bought. Fourth, it is a charge against revenue, so it reduces the profit of the year.

slides.heading: Quick check: what is depreciation?
slides.body_md: Choose the term for spreading the depreciable cost of a fixed asset over its useful life.
slides.narration: Think about what happens to the cost of a machine, less any amount expected at the end, over the years in which it serves the business. Is the cost rising, being revalued, or being spread?

visual.caption: Four causes of depreciation.

slides.narration: There are four causes. Wear and tear comes from the use of the asset, from weather and from age. Expiry of legal rights affects a lease, a patent or a licence, which comes to an end after a fixed period. Obsolescence happens when new technology makes the asset out of date. Abnormal factors are events such as an accident, a fire, a flood or a theft.

slides.heading: Why depreciation must be charged

rows: The asset helps earn revenue for several years, so each year bears a part of its cost
The balance sheet should not show the asset at more than its worth to the business
Profit not withdrawn because of the charge stays in the business and can help replace the asset
Depreciation is allowed as a charge in working out taxable profit, within the rules

visual.alt: Table of five needs for charging depreciation

slides.narration: Depreciation must be charged for five reasons. It matches the cost of the asset with the revenue it helps earn. It gives the true profit, since ignoring it overstates profit. It gives a true financial position, since the asset is not shown at more than its worth. It keeps profit in the business, which can help replace the asset. And it is allowed as a charge when taxable profit is worked out.

slides.heading: Quick check: is depreciation a cash expense?
slides.body_md: True or false: the depreciation charged for a year is paid out in cash during that year.
slides.narration: Ask when the cash for the asset was actually paid. Does anything further leave the cash book when the yearly charge is made?

slides.heading: Factors that fix the amount

rows: Price paid plus carriage, installation and other costs of making it ready for use
Estimated amount the asset will fetch at the end of its life, net of selling costs
Estimated number of years the asset will serve the business

visual.alt: Table of four factors that fix the amount of depreciation, with the figures of an imagined firm, Rana Engineering: cost 5,00,000, residual value 1,00,000, depreciable cost 4,00,000, life 5 years

slides.narration: Four factors fix the amount of depreciation. The cost includes the price paid and the cost of making the asset ready for use. The estimated residual value is what the asset will fetch at the end of its life. The depreciable cost is the cost less the residual value. The estimated useful life is the number of years the asset will serve. For Rana Engineering, the cost is five lakh rupees and the residual value is one lakh rupees.

slides.heading: The straight line method

rows: Yearly depreciation as a per cent of original cost
The same amount, a fixed instalment
Falls by an equal amount each year

visual.alt: Table: the straight line method, with the figures of Rana Engineering

slides.narration: Under the straight line method, the same amount is charged every year. Yearly depreciation is the cost less the residual value, divided by the estimated life. It can also be stated as a rate on the original cost. For Rana Engineering the depreciable cost is rupees four lakh and the life is five years, so the yearly depreciation is rupees eighty thousand. That is sixteen per cent of the cost.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: Rana Engineering
slides.body_md: A machine costs **₹5,00,000**, has a residual value of **₹1,00,000** and a life of **5 years**. Show the book value year by year.

visual.alt: Straight line depreciation schedule of Rana Engineering over five years: 80,000 each year, book value falling from 5,00,000 to 1,00,000

slides.narration: Each year the charge is rupees eighty thousand. The book value starts at rupees five lakh and falls by that amount every year. After five years it is rupees one lakh, which is exactly the residual value. The charge never changes, so the book value falls in a straight line.

slides.heading: Quick check: yearly depreciation
slides.body_md: Find the yearly depreciation of an imagined bottling line under the straight line method.
slides.narration: First deduct the residual value from the cost to get the depreciable cost. Then divide by the number of years of life.

slides.heading: Straight line method: merits and limits

rows: Ignores the fact that repairs rise as the asset ages
The charge is the same every year, so profits are not distorted by changes in the charge
The same charge on a falling book value means a rising rate on the value still in the books
The asset can be written down to its residual value or to nil
Does not take into account the interest lost on the money tied up in the asset

visual.alt: Table of merits and limits of the straight line method

slides.narration: The straight line method is simple to understand and to apply. Since the charge is the same each year, profit is not disturbed by a change in the charge, and the asset can be written down to its residual value or to nil. Its limits are that it ignores the rise in repairs as the asset ages, and it takes no account of the interest lost on the money tied up in the asset.

slides.heading: The written down value method

rows: Rate per cent × opening book value of the year
Opening book value, which falls every year
Highest in the first year and falling every year
Falls every year but never reaches nil

visual.alt: Table: the written down value method

slides.narration: Under the written down value method, a fixed rate is applied to the opening book value of each year. In the first year the book value is the cost, so the charge is the same as under the straight line method at the same rate. After that the book value falls, so the charge falls too. The book value goes down every year but never reaches nil.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Sunder Tools
slides.body_md: A machine of **Sunder Tools**, an imagined firm, costs **₹2,00,000** and is depreciated at **15%** a year on the written down value.

visual.alt: Written down value depreciation schedule of an imagined firm, Sunder Tools, over three years at 15 per cent: charges 30,000, 25,500 and 21,675, closing book value 1,22,825

slides.narration: In the first year the charge is fifteen per cent of rupees two lakh, which is rupees thirty thousand. The book value becomes rupees one lakh seventy thousand. In the second year the charge is fifteen per cent of that, rupees twenty five thousand five hundred. In the third year it is rupees twenty one thousand six hundred seventy five, and the book value at the end is rupees one lakh twenty two thousand eight hundred twenty five.

slides.heading: Quick check: third-year charge
slides.body_md: Find the depreciation of an imagined loom for the third year by the written down value method.
slides.narration: Apply the rate to the opening book value of each year. Work through the first and second years before the third.

slides.heading: Written down value method: merits and limits

rows: The heavy charge in the early years is met by the low repairs of a new asset
The book value never falls to nil or to the residual value
The total of depreciation and repairs is more even from year to year
The calculation is harder than for the straight line method
Most of the cost is written off in the early years, which suits assets that lose value quickly
The charge in the later years can become very small

visual.alt: Table of merits and limits of the written down value method

slides.narration: The heavy charge of the early years is met by the low repairs of a new asset, and the light charge of the later years sits beside the higher repairs. So the total burden of depreciation and repairs is more even. Most of the cost is written off early, which suits assets that lose value quickly. The limits are that the book value never reaches nil, the calculation is harder, and the late charge can become very small.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an asset bought during the year
slides.body_md: **Tilak Presses**, an imagined firm with books closing on 31 March, bought a machine for **₹2,40,000** on **1 July 2026**. Depreciation is 10% a year.

visual.alt: Depreciation of a machine of an imagined firm, Tilak Presses, bought for 2,40,000 on 1 July 2026 at 10% a year: first year (9 months) 18,000 under both methods; second year 24,000 under the straight line method and 22,200 under the written down value method

slides.narration: The machine was used for nine months in the first year, from the first of July to the thirty first of March. The charge is nine twelfths of ten per cent of the cost, which is rupees eighteen thousand under both methods. In the second year, the straight line method charges rupees twenty four thousand and the written down value method charges rupees twenty two thousand two hundred.

slides.heading: Straight line against written down value

rows: Can reach the residual value or nil
Total burden of depreciation and repairs rises with age

visual.alt: Table comparing the straight line and written down value methods on five points

slides.narration: The two methods differ in five ways. The straight line method applies the rate to original cost, and the written down value method applies it to the opening book value. The first charges equally every year and the second charges less each year. The first can reach nil, while the second never does. The second gives a more even total of depreciation and repairs. And the second is harder to calculate.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Depreciation spreads the depreciable cost of a fixed asset over its useful life; it is a non-cash charge against revenue.
Straight line: (cost − residual value) ÷ life; the charge is equal each year.
Written down value: a rate on the opening book value; the charge falls each year.

rows: Fall in the book value of a fixed asset; its depreciable cost spread over its life; non-cash
Wear and tear, expiry of legal rights, obsolescence, abnormal factors
(Cost − residual value) ÷ life, or a rate on cost; equal charge each year
A rate on the opening book value; falling charge; never nil
Charge from the date of purchase to the year end, or to the date of sale

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1

slides.narration: To sum up. Depreciation is the decline in the book value of a fixed asset, and accounting spreads its depreciable cost over its useful life. It arises from wear and tear, expiry of legal rights, obsolescence and abnormal factors. The straight line method charges the same amount every year. The written down value method applies a rate to the opening book value, so the charge falls. A part of a year gets a part of the charge.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Count the months from the date of purchase.
State the base of the rate: cost, or opening book value.

rows: Show the formula and the substitution
Method marks are given even when a figure is wrong
Count the months from the date of purchase
A part-year gets a part-year charge
Apply the written down value rate to the opening book value
Not to the cost, except in the first year
State the base of the rate
Cost for the straight line method; book value for the written down value method

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 1

slides.narration: In the examination, write the formula and then substitute the figures, because method marks are given even when a figure is wrong. Count the months from the date of purchase when an asset is bought during the year. Apply the written down value rate to the opening book value, not to the cost, except in the first year. And always say what the rate is applied to.

slides.body_md: Part 2: **recording** depreciation, the **sale** of an asset, **provisions** and **reserves**.

Profit or loss on sale is found

visual.caption: From purchase to sale of a machine.

slides.narration: Once the amount of depreciation is known, it must be recorded in the books. In this part we see two ways of recording it, and we follow a machine from its purchase to its sale, finding the profit or loss on the sale. We end with provisions and reserves, two ideas that are often confused. We work with imagined firms such as Asha Printers, Bhavani Looms and Chitra Packaging.

visual.caption: Two ways of recording the same depreciation.

slides.narration: There are two ways. In the first, depreciation is credited to the asset account, which falls to its book value. In the second, depreciation is credited to a provision for depreciation account, and the asset account stays at cost. In the balance sheet, the provision is deducted from the cost. In the first year of Asha Printers, both ways show the same book value of rupees five lakh eighty eight thousand.

slides.narration: The purchase entry is the same in both ways. For the yearly depreciation, the expense account is debited. slides.heading: Worked example 1: Asha Printers, the working
slides.body_md: **Asha Printers**, an imagined firm, bought Machine A for **₹4,00,000** on 1 April 2025 and Machine B for **₹2,40,000** on 1 October 2025. Depreciation is **10% on cost**; books close on 31 March; Machine B is sold on 1 January 2028.

visual.alt: Depreciation of Asha Printers by year and machine: 52,000 in 2025–26, 64,000 in 2026–27 and 58,000 in 2027–28, with Machine B depreciated for 6 months, 12 months and 9 months

slides.narration: Machine A is charged rupees forty thousand a year. Machine B is used for six months in the first year, which is rupees twelve thousand, then for a full year, rupees twenty four thousand, and for nine months in the third year, up to the date of sale, rupees eighteen thousand. The yearly totals are rupees fifty two thousand, rupees sixty four thousand and rupees fifty eight thousand.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the Machinery Account in the year of sale
slides.body_md: Machine B is sold for **₹1,80,000**. Its book value at the date of sale is **₹1,86,000**, so there is a loss on sale of **₹6,000**.

rows: By Bank A/c (sale of Machine B, 1 January 2028)
By Profit and Loss A/c (loss on sale of Machine B)

visual.alt: Machinery A/c of Asha Printers for the year ended 31 March 2028 under the direct method: balance brought down 5,24,000; depreciation 58,000; sale of Machine B 1,80,000; loss on sale 6,000; balance carried down 2,80,000

slides.narration: The account opens with the balance brought down of rupees five lakh twenty four thousand. On the credit side we write the depreciation of the year, rupees fifty eight thousand, the sale proceeds of rupees one lakh eighty thousand, and the loss on sale of rupees six thousand. The balance carried down is rupees two lakh eighty thousand, which is the book value of Machine A alone.

slides.heading: Sale of an asset: the steps

rows: Charge depreciation on the asset sold from the start of the year up to the date of sale
Find the book value at the date of sale: cost less depreciation to that date
Compare the sale proceeds with the book value: more is a profit, less is a loss
Record the sale in the Machinery A/c, or in an Asset Disposal A/c if a provision account is kept
Transfer the profit or loss to the Profit and Loss A/c

visual.alt: Table of five steps in accounting for the sale of an asset

slides.narration: When an asset is sold, first charge depreciation on it up to the date of sale. Then find the book value at that date, which is the cost less the depreciation so far. Compare the sale proceeds with the book value. If the proceeds are more, there is a profit, and if they are less, there is a loss. Record the sale and transfer the profit or loss to the profit and loss account.

slides.narration: The part year charge comes first. Then the cost and the accumulated depreciation go to the disposal account. The balancing profit or loss goes last.

By Profit and Loss A/c (loss on sale of Machine B)

rows: Machines at original cost: purchases on the debit side, cost of machines sold on the credit side
Cost of the machines in hand

visual.alt: Table of the three accounts used in the provision method

slides.narration: With a provision account, three accounts are used. The machinery account stays at cost and closes at the cost of the machines in hand. The provision for depreciation account collects the depreciation of each year, and loses the share of a machine that is sold. The asset disposal account brings together the cost, the accumulated depreciation and the sale proceeds of the machine sold, and it closes with a nil balance.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the Provision for Depreciation Account
slides.body_md: **Chitra Packaging**, an imagined firm, bought Machine A for ₹6,00,000 and Machine B for ₹1,20,000 in 2025, at 10% on cost; Machine B is sold on 1 October 2026 for **₹1,10,000**.

visual.alt: Provision for Depreciation A/c of Chitra Packaging for the year ended 31 March 2027: balance brought down 69,000; depreciation 66,000; accumulated depreciation of Machine B 15,000 transferred to Asset Disposal A/c; balance carried down 1,20,000

slides.narration: The provision account opens with rupees sixty nine thousand. The depreciation of the year, rupees sixty six thousand, is added on the credit side. The accumulated depreciation of Machine B, rupees fifteen thousand, is transferred to the asset disposal account on the debit side. The balance carried down is rupees one lakh twenty thousand, which belongs to Machine A.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: the Asset Disposal Account
slides.body_md: Machine B: cost **₹1,20,000**, accumulated depreciation **₹15,000**, book value **₹1,05,000**, sold for **₹1,10,000**.

rows: To Profit and Loss A/c (profit on sale)

visual.alt: Asset Disposal A/c of Chitra Packaging: cost of Machine B 1,20,000 debited; accumulated depreciation 15,000 and sale proceeds 1,10,000 credited; profit on sale 5,000 debited and transferred to Profit and Loss A/c

slides.narration: The cost of rupees one lakh twenty thousand is debited to the account. The accumulated depreciation of rupees fifteen thousand and the sale proceeds of rupees one lakh ten thousand are credited. The debit side is higher, so the balancing figure of rupees five thousand, a profit on sale, is written on the debit side and transferred to the profit and loss account. The account closes.

visual.alt: Table: treatment of an addition during the year and of a sale of part of the assets, with Asha Printers as the example

slides.narration: When an asset is added during the year, depreciation is charged only from the date of purchase to the year end. When part of the assets is sold, depreciation on that part is charged up to the date of sale, and only its cost and its accumulated depreciation leave the accounts. In Asha Printers, Machine B was charged for six months in the year it was bought and nine months in the year it was sold.

slides.heading: What is a provision?

rows: The fall in the value of a fixed asset is certain, but the exact yearly amount rests on estimates
Some debtors may not pay; the provision is named here and its adjustments come in a later chapter
Tax on the profit of the year is payable later, and its final amount is not yet known
A large repair is certain in a later year, and its cost is estimated

visual.alt: Table of examples of provisions and the reason for each

slides.narration: A provision is an amount charged against profit for a known liability or loss whose exact amount cannot be stated. Examples are depreciation, doubtful debts, taxation and repairs. The provision for doubtful debts is only named here, and the adjustments for it are taken up in a later chapter. A provision is a charge, so it reduces the profit of the year.

slides.heading: Differences between provisions and reserves

rows: Deducted from the asset or shown among the liabilities
To meet a known liability or loss
Must be made even when there is no profit
Created only out of profit, and by choice

visual.alt: Table of five differences between a provision and a reserve

slides.narration: Provisions and reserves differ in five ways. A provision is a charge against profit, and a reserve is an appropriation of profit. A provision reduces the profit, and a reserve does not reduce the profit earned. A provision is deducted from the asset or shown among the liabilities, and a reserve is shown with the owners funds. A provision meets a known liability, and a reserve strengthens the business. A provision must be made even if there is no profit, but a reserve needs profit.

slides.heading: Types of reserves

rows: Revenue reserve out of profit, with no stated purpose
Meena Foods keeps back ₹18,000 of its profit
Revenue reserve for a stated purpose
Dividend equalisation reserve, to even out payouts
Reserve out of a capital profit
Profit on the sale of a fixed asset kept as a reserve
Reserve not shown in the balance sheet
Stock shown below its true value

visual.alt: Table of types of reserves with meaning and example

slides.narration: Revenue reserves are made out of trading profit. A general reserve has no stated purpose, and a specific reserve has one, for example a dividend equalisation reserve. A capital reserve is made out of a capital profit, such as a profit on the sale of a fixed asset. A secret reserve is not shown in the balance sheet, and it can be built by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities.

slides.heading: Importance of reserves

rows: The business has a cushion that outsiders can see and trust
Losses can be met without borrowing or without a call on the owner
Profit kept back gives funds to buy assets without a loan
A specific reserve helps the owners to be paid steadily in lean years

visual.alt: Table of four reasons why reserves are important

slides.narration: Reserves are important for four reasons. They give the business a stronger position that outsiders can see. They help to meet unexpected losses without borrowing. They provide funds for expansion, since profit kept back can buy assets without a loan. And a specific reserve helps the owners to be paid steadily in lean years.

sections.heading: 1. Depreciation: meaning and features
sections.body_md:
**Depreciation** is the decline in the book value of a fixed asset through use, the passage of time or obsolescence. In accounting it means spreading the **depreciable cost** of the asset over its **useful life**, as an expense charged against the revenue of each year.

**Features:** (1) it is a decline in book value; (2) it applies to fixed assets only; (3) it is a non-cash expense, since the cash was paid when the asset was bought; (4) it is a charge against revenue, so it reduces profit.

key_terms.definition_md: A long-lived resource that the business holds for use in its operations, not for sale in the ordinary course, for example machinery or furniture.
The decline in the book value of a fixed asset through use, the passage of time or obsolescence; the allocation of its depreciable cost over its useful life.
The cost of an asset less the depreciation charged on it up to a date; also called the written down value.
An expense, such as depreciation, whose charge needs no payment of cash in the year it is charged.

sections.heading: 2. Causes, need and the factors that fix the amount
sections.body_md:
**Causes:** wear and tear; expiry of legal rights (a lease, patent or licence); obsolescence; abnormal factors such as accident, fire, flood or theft.

**Need:** matching of cost with revenue; true profit; true financial position; replacement funds; tax considerations.

**Factors:** the cost of the asset, its estimated residual value, its depreciable cost (cost less residual value) and its estimated useful life.

key_terms.definition_md: The cost of an asset less its estimated residual value; the amount to be spread over the useful life.
The estimated amount that an asset will fetch at the end of its useful life, after deducting the expected cost of selling it; also called scrap or salvage value.
The estimated period, in years, over which an asset is expected to serve the business.
Loss of the usefulness of an asset because newer technology or a change in demand has made it out of date.

sections.heading: 3. Straight line method
sections.body_md:
Under the **straight line method** (fixed instalment method) the same amount is charged every year: **yearly depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ estimated life**, or a fixed rate on the original cost.

Rana Engineering: (5,00,000 − 1,00,000) ÷ 5 = ₹80,000 a year, which is 16% of cost.

**Merits:** simple; equal charge; asset can be written down to the residual value or nil. **Limits:** ignores rising repairs; ignores interest on the money tied up.

key_terms.definition_md: A method of depreciation that charges the same amount in each full year, found by dividing the depreciable cost by the estimated life or by applying a fixed rate to original cost.

The charge is the same every year, so profits are not distorted by changes in the charge
The same charge on a falling book value means a rising rate on the value still in the books
The asset can be written down to its residual value or to nil
Does not take into account the interest lost on the money tied up in the asset

sections.heading: 4. Written down value method and comparison
sections.body_md:
Under the **written down value method** (diminishing balance method) a fixed rate is applied to the **opening book value** of each year, so the charge falls every year and the book value never reaches nil.

Sunder Tools, 15% on 2,00,000: 30,000, 25,500, 21,675.

**Part of a year:** an asset bought or sold during the year is charged for the months of use, rate × months ÷ 12.

**Comparison:** the straight line method charges on cost and equally; the written down value method charges on the book value and less each year. At the same rate the first-year charges are equal.

key_terms.definition_md: A method of depreciation that applies a fixed rate to the opening book value of each year, so the yearly charge falls.

sections.heading: 5. Recording depreciation
sections.body_md:
**Two ways.** (1) Charge depreciation to the **asset account**: Depreciation A/c Dr., To Machinery A/c; the asset is shown at book value. (2) Create a **provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account**: Depreciation A/c Dr., To Provision for Depreciation A/c; the asset stays at cost and the provision is deducted from it.

In both ways the Depreciation A/c is closed by **Profit and Loss A/c Dr., To Depreciation A/c**.

**Sale of part of the assets:** only the cost and depreciation of that part leave the accounts. **Addition:** depreciation from the date of purchase.

sections.heading: 7. Provisions and reserves
sections.body_md:
A **provision** is an amount charged against profit for a known liability or loss whose amount cannot be stated exactly (depreciation, doubtful debts, taxation, repairs). A **reserve** is an appropriation of profit kept back to strengthen the business.

**Reserves:** revenue reserves (general reserve, with no stated purpose, and specific reserve, for a stated purpose such as dividend equalisation); capital reserve (from a capital profit such as a gain on the sale of a fixed asset); secret reserve (not shown in the balance sheet).

**Importance of reserves:** stronger position, meeting unexpected losses, expansion, even payouts.

The provision for doubtful debts is only named here.

key_terms.definition_md: An amount charged against profit for a known liability or an expected loss whose exact amount cannot be determined.
A part of profit that is retained in the business, by appropriation, to strengthen its financial position.
A revenue reserve created out of profit without any particular purpose.
A revenue reserve created out of profit for a stated purpose, for example a dividend equalisation reserve.
A reserve created out of a capital profit, for example the profit on the sale of a fixed asset.
A reserve that is not disclosed in the balance sheet, created by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Depreciation: write the formula, substitute, and count the months for a part-year.
- Straight line: rate on cost, equal charge. Written down value: rate on opening book value, falling charge.
- Direct method: Depreciation A/c Dr., To Machinery A/c. Provision method: Depreciation A/c Dr., To Provision for Depreciation A/c; asset at cost.
- Always close the Depreciation A/c by a transfer to the Profit and Loss A/c.
- On sale: depreciation to the date of sale, book value, then sale proceeds less book value.
- Balance every account with To and By lines; the Asset Disposal A/c must close.
- Provision: a charge against profit. Reserve: an appropriation of profit. Never mix them.

cards.back_md: The decline in the book value of a fixed asset through use, the passage of time or obsolescence; its depreciable cost is spread over its useful life.
Decline in book value; applies to fixed assets; non-cash expense; charge against revenue.
Wear and tear; expiry of legal rights; obsolescence; abnormal factors such as accident or fire.
Matching; true profit; true financial position; replacement funds; tax considerations.
Cost of the asset less its estimated residual value.
The estimated amount an asset will fetch at the end of its useful life, net of selling costs; scrap or salvage value.
Cost less the depreciation charged up to a date; the written down value.

cards.front_md: Factors that fix the amount of depreciation
cards.back_md: Cost; estimated residual value; depreciable cost; estimated useful life.
Equal charge each year: (cost − residual value) ÷ life, or a fixed rate on original cost.
Yearly depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ estimated life.

cards.front_md: Rate of the straight line method
cards.back_md: Yearly depreciation ÷ original cost × 100.
A fixed rate on the opening book value of each year; the charge falls; the book value never reaches nil.
Rate × opening book value of the year.

cards.front_md: Merits of the straight line method
cards.back_md: Simple; equal charge; asset can be written down to the residual value or nil.

cards.front_md: Limits of the straight line method
cards.back_md: Ignores rising repairs; ignores interest on the money tied up in the asset.

cards.front_md: Merits of the written down value method
cards.back_md: Heavy charge when repairs are low, light charge when repairs are high; more even total burden.

cards.front_md: Limit of the written down value method
cards.back_md: Book value never reaches nil; harder to calculate; late charges become very small.
Charge = yearly depreciation × months of use ÷ 12, from the date of purchase or to the date of sale.

cards.front_md: First-year charge at the same rate
cards.back_md: Equal under both methods, because the opening book value is the cost.
Credit the asset account; or credit a Provision for Depreciation A/c and keep the asset at cost.

cards.front_md: Entry: depreciation charged to the asset account
cards.back_md: Depreciation A/c Dr., To Asset A/c.
Depreciation A/c Dr., To Provision for Depreciation A/c.
Profit and Loss A/c Dr., To Depreciation A/c.

cards.front_md: Balance sheet under the provision method
cards.back_md: The asset at original cost, with the provision for depreciation deducted from it.
Temporary account that brings together cost, accumulated depreciation and sale proceeds of an asset to find the profit or loss on sale; it closes at nil.
Sale proceeds − book value at the date of sale; positive is profit, negative is loss.

cards.front_md: Book value at the date of sale
cards.back_md: Cost − depreciation up to the date of sale, including the part-year charge.

cards.front_md: Sale of part of the assets
cards.back_md: Only the cost and the depreciation of the part sold leave the accounts.
An amount charged against profit for a known liability or loss of uncertain amount; examples: depreciation, doubtful debts, taxation, repairs.
A part of profit kept back in the business to strengthen it; an appropriation of profit.

cards.front_md: Provision against reserve: effect on profit
cards.back_md: A provision reduces the profit; a reserve is set aside out of the profit already found.
General; specific; capital; secret.
A reserve not disclosed in the balance sheet, created by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities.

questions.stem_md: Gauri Textiles, an imagined firm in the imagined town of Sonpur, spreads the cost of its weaving machines, less any amount expected at the end, over the years in which the machines will serve the business. This process is called

options.text_md: appreciation
depreciation
amortisation of goodwill only
revaluation of the machines

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** depreciation. The allocation of the depreciable cost of a fixed asset over its useful life is depreciation. Appreciation is a rise in value, goodwill is not a machine, and revaluation means restating the value of an asset to a new figure.

questions.stem_md: Tarun Studio, an imagined photo studio, replaced its working camera printers with newer models after a new printing technology made them out of date, although they had many years of physical life left. The cause of depreciation here is

options.text_md: wear and tear
expiry of legal rights
an accident
obsolescence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** obsolescence. An asset that loses its usefulness because newer technology has replaced it is affected by obsolescence. The printers were still in working order, so wear and tear does not apply, no legal right ran out, and nothing abnormal such as an accident happened.

questions.stem_md: Pushkar Quarries, an imagined firm, took a mining lease for 15 years at a cost of ₹9,00,000 and spreads the cost over the 15 years of the lease. The cause of depreciation is

options.text_md: expiry of legal rights
obsolescence
wear and tear
abnormal factors such as fire

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** expiry of legal rights. A lease, patent or similar right is valid only for a fixed period, and its value falls to nothing when the period ends. That is a fall through the expiry of legal rights. The lease is not damaged by use, is not outdated by technology and has not been hit by an accident.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about depreciation in the books of Lohit Foundry, an imagined firm, is correct?

options.text_md: It is paid in cash to the supplier of the asset every year
It is a gain that increases the profit of the year
It is charged against revenue but no cash leaves the business when it is charged
It is charged only in the years in which the asset is sold

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is charged against revenue but no cash leaves the business when it is charged. The cash for the asset was paid when it was bought. The yearly charge only spreads that cost against the revenue of each year, so it reduces profit without any cash outflow. It is neither a yearly payment, nor a gain, nor a charge made only on sale.

questions.stem_md: While deciding the yearly depreciation on a new lathe, Hari Tools, an imagined workshop, considers all of the following. Which one is NOT a factor that fixes the amount of depreciation?

options.text_md: The cost of the lathe
The estimated residual value of the lathe
The selling price of the goods the lathe produces
The estimated useful life of the lathe

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The selling price of the goods the lathe produces. The amount of depreciation depends on the cost, the estimated residual value and the estimated useful life. The selling price of the goods produced affects profit, but it plays no part in working out depreciation.

questions.stem_md: Saket Dyes, an imagined firm, buys a dyeing machine for ₹3,60,000. It expects the machine to work for 5 years and to be worth ₹60,000 at the end. Under the straight line method, the yearly depreciation is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹60,000. Depreciable cost is 3,60,000 − 60,000 = 3,00,000, and 3,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹60,000. The figure ₹72,000 ignores the residual value, ₹84,000 adds the residual value instead of deducting it, and ₹12,000 divides only the residual value by the life.

questions.stem_md: Tulsi Cycles, an imagined firm, buys a machine for ₹2,00,000 and depreciates it at 10% a year by the written down value method. The depreciation for the second year is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹18,000. The first-year charge is 10% of 2,00,000 = 20,000, which leaves a book value of 1,80,000. The second-year charge is 10% of that book value, ₹18,000. The figure ₹20,000 is the straight line charge on cost, ₹38,000 is the two years added together, and ₹15,000 is a nine-month charge on cost.

questions.stem_md: Under the straight line method, the depreciation charged to an asset of Veena Mills, an imagined firm, in each full year of its life is

options.text_md: higher in the early years and lower in the later years
the same amount, because it is a fixed share of cost
lower in the early years and higher in the later years
a fixed per cent of the opening book value

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the same amount, because it is a fixed share of cost. The straight line method applies a fixed rate to the original cost, or divides the depreciable cost equally over the life, so each full year bears the same charge. A falling charge belongs to the written down value method, which works on the opening book value.

questions.stem_md: Under the written down value method, the yearly charge on a machine of Ganga Press, an imagined firm, falls from year to year because the rate is applied to

options.text_md: the book value at the start of each year
the original cost every year
the residual value of the machine
the total depreciation charged so far

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the book value at the start of each year. The rate is applied to the opening book value, and the book value falls each year as depreciation is deducted, so the charge falls too. Applying the rate to original cost would give an equal charge, which is the straight line method.

questions.stem_md: Rupa Looms, an imagined firm, finds that the repair bills of its machines rise steadily as the machines age. It wants the total of depreciation and repairs charged to profit to stay fairly level from year to year. Which method of depreciation suits this aim better, and why?

options.text_md: Straight line, because the rising repairs offset the rising depreciation
Written down value, because the falling depreciation offsets the rising repairs
Written down value, because it charges nothing in the first year
Straight line, because it charges less than the other method in every year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Written down value, because the falling depreciation offsets the rising repairs. Under the written down value method the depreciation is heavy in the early years, when repairs are low, and light in the later years, when repairs are high, so the total burden stays more even. Under the straight line method depreciation is constant, so the total burden rises with repairs. Neither method charges nothing in the first year, and the straight line method does not charge less in every year.

questions.stem_md: Dhruv Engineering, an imagined firm, buys a press for ₹5,00,000 and is deciding between the straight line method and the written down value method, each at 20% a year. For the first year of the press, the two methods give

options.text_md: a higher charge under the straight line method
a higher charge under the written down value method
the same charge of ₹1,00,000
no charge under the written down value method

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the same charge of ₹1,00,000. In the first year the opening book value equals the cost, so 20% of 5,00,000 = 1,00,000 under both methods. The two charges separate from the second year, when the written down value method charges 80,000 against 1,00,000.

questions.stem_md: Naman Packers, an imagined firm, whose books close on 31 March, bought a machine for ₹1,80,000 on 1 August 2026 and depreciates machinery at 10% a year on cost. The depreciation for the year ended 31 March 2027 is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹12,000. The machine was used from 1 August to 31 March, which is 8 months, so the charge is 1,80,000 × 10% × 8/12 = ₹12,000. The full-year charge ₹18,000 ignores the date of purchase, and ₹15,000 and ₹9,000 count ten months and six months.

questions.stem_md: Deepa Looms, an imagined firm, records depreciation by crediting a Provision for Depreciation A/c each year. In its balance sheet the machinery account is shown at

options.text_md: cost less depreciation, with no provision shown
the market value of the machines
the residual value of the machines
cost, with the provision shown as a deduction from it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** cost, with the provision shown as a deduction from it. When a provision account is kept, the asset account stays at original cost and the accumulated depreciation is shown as a deduction, so the net figure is the book value. Showing cost less depreciation with no provision is the direct method, and neither market value nor residual value is used.

questions.stem_md: Ishaan Moulds, an imagined firm, charges depreciation directly to its Machinery A/c. The journal entry for the yearly depreciation is

options.text_md: Machinery A/c Dr. To Depreciation A/c
Depreciation A/c Dr. To Provision for Depreciation A/c
Depreciation A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Depreciation A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c. Depreciation is an expense, so it is debited, and the asset falls in value, so the Machinery A/c is credited. The second entry has the sides reversed, the third belongs to the provision method, and the last one skips the Depreciation A/c, through which the charge is normally passed on to profit and loss.

questions.stem_md: Jayant Fabrics, an imagined firm, keeps a Provision for Depreciation A/c. The entry that records the yearly depreciation is

options.text_md: Depreciation A/c Dr. To Machinery A/c
Depreciation A/c Dr. To Provision for Depreciation A/c
Provision for Depreciation A/c Dr. To Depreciation A/c
Machinery A/c Dr. To Provision for Depreciation A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Depreciation A/c Dr. To Provision for Depreciation A/c. The expense is debited and the provision is credited, while the Machinery A/c is left untouched at cost. The second entry reduces the asset itself, the third reverses the sides, and the last would raise the cost of the machinery.

questions.stem_md: At the end of the year, the Depreciation A/c of Kesar Mills, an imagined firm, is closed by transferring its balance to the

options.text_md: debit side of the Profit and Loss A/c
credit side of the Profit and Loss A/c
debit side of the Capital A/c
credit side of the Machinery A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** debit side of the Profit and Loss A/c. Depreciation is an expense of the year, so its balance goes to the debit of the Profit and Loss A/c, by the entry Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Depreciation A/c. It is not an appropriation against capital, and it is not credited again to the asset.

questions.stem_md: Lalit Plastics, an imagined firm, keeps a Provision for Depreciation A/c and sells one of its machines during the year. The profit or loss on the sale is found by opening an

options.text_md: Suspense A/c
Asset Disposal A/c
Drawings A/c
Capital Reserve A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Asset Disposal A/c. When the asset stays at cost in its account, its cost, its accumulated depreciation and its sale proceeds are brought together in an Asset Disposal A/c, and the balancing figure is the profit or loss on sale. A suspense account holds an unexplained difference, and drawings and a capital reserve have nothing to do with the sale.

questions.stem_md: Neel Looms, an imagined firm, sells a machine that cost ₹1,50,000 and on which ₹60,000 of depreciation has been provided up to the date of sale. The sale price is ₹80,000. The result of the sale is

options.text_md: a profit of ₹10,000
a loss of ₹70,000
a profit of ₹20,000
a loss of ₹10,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a loss of ₹10,000. Book value = 1,50,000 − 60,000 = 90,000. The machine is sold for 80,000, which is 10,000 less than the book value, so there is a loss of ₹10,000. A loss of ₹70,000 compares the sale price with cost and ignores the depreciation already charged.

questions.stem_md: Mahesh Crafts, an imagined firm whose books close on 31 March, sold a machine on 1 October 2027. Depreciation on that machine for the year ended 31 March 2028 is charged for

options.text_md: 6 months, from 1 April to 30 September
12 months, as the machine was in the books at the start of the year
5 months, from 1 October to 31 March
no period, since the machine is no longer owned

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 6 months, from 1 April to 30 September. Depreciation is charged up to the date of sale, which is the six months from 1 April to 30 September, so that the book value at sale is right. A full year would overcharge the machine, five months counts the period after the sale, and charging nothing would leave the book value too high.

questions.stem_md: Asha Printers, an imagined firm, buys Machine A for ₹4,00,000 on 1 April 2025 and Machine B for ₹2,40,000 on 1 October 2025, and depreciates at 10% a year on cost under the provision method. The balance of its Provision for Depreciation A/c on 31 March 2027 is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹1,16,000. Year 1 charge: 52,000; year 2 charge: 64,000. The provision is the two charges added, ₹1,16,000. The figure ₹64,000 is only the second year, ₹5,24,000 is the book value, which the provision does not show, and ₹52,000 is only the first year.

questions.stem_md: Under the provision method, a machine of Omkar Plastics, an imagined firm, is sold at a loss. In the Asset Disposal A/c the cost of the machine and the loss on sale appear, respectively, on the

options.text_md: credit side and debit side
debit side and debit side
debit side and credit side
credit side and credit side

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** debit side and credit side. The cost of the machine is debited to the Asset Disposal A/c, as it is transferred out of the Machinery A/c. The accumulated depreciation and the sale proceeds are credited, and when these fall short of cost the shortfall, the loss, is credited to balance the account and moved to the debit of the Profit and Loss A/c.

questions.stem_md: Pranav Provisions, an imagined firm, charges ₹15,000 against its profit for repairs that it knows it will have to bear but whose exact cost is not yet known. This amount is a

options.text_md: provision
reserve
drawing
capital receipt

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** provision. An amount charged against profit for a known liability or loss whose amount cannot be stated exactly is a provision. A reserve is a part of profit kept back, drawings are the owner taking money out, and a capital receipt is money brought in as capital.

questions.stem_md: Rohini Dairy, an imagined firm, sets aside ₹40,000 of its profit to meet a possible dip in future payouts to its owners. Such a reserve, kept for a stated purpose, is a

options.text_md: general reserve
capital reserve
secret reserve
specific reserve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** specific reserve. A revenue reserve created for a particular purpose, such as evening out future payouts, is a specific reserve. A general reserve has no stated purpose, a capital reserve comes out of capital profit, and a secret reserve is not shown in the books at all.

questions.stem_md: Sudha Traders, an imagined firm, sold a plot of land for ₹3,50,000 more than its book value. The profit is a capital profit, and the firm decides to keep it in a reserve. The reserve is a

options.text_md: general reserve
capital reserve
specific reserve
secret reserve

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** capital reserve. A reserve built out of a capital profit, such as the profit on the sale of a fixed asset, is a capital reserve. General and specific reserves come from the ordinary trading profit, and a secret reserve is hidden from the balance sheet.

questions.stem_md: Tarini Silks, an imagined firm, writes down the value of its stock in the balance sheet below its true value, which builds a reserve that the balance sheet does not disclose. This is a

options.text_md: secret reserve
capital reserve
general reserve
provision for doubtful debts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** secret reserve. A reserve that does not appear in the balance sheet, created by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities, is a secret reserve. Capital and general reserves are shown openly, and a provision for doubtful debts is a charge for a likely loss on debtors.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a provision from a reserve in the books of Uma Stores, an imagined firm?

options.text_md: A provision is an appropriation of profit, while a reserve is a charge against profit
A provision is charged before the profit is found, while a reserve is set aside out of profit already found
A provision is never shown in the balance sheet, while a reserve always is
A provision strengthens the business, while a reserve meets a known liability

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A provision is charged before the profit is found, while a reserve is set aside out of profit already found. A provision reduces the profit, because it is charged against it, while a reserve is part of the profit kept back after it has been found. The second statement reverses the two, a provision is shown in the balance sheet, and the purposes in the last option are also reversed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When Wasim Tools, an imagined firm, charges depreciation on its machines, its profit falls but its cash balance does not.

**Reason (R):** Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset that was already paid for, so no cash goes out when it is charged.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. The cash was paid when the machine was bought, and the yearly charge only moves part of that cost to the profit and loss account, which explains why the cash balance stays the same.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under the written down value method, the depreciation charged is highest in the first year of the asset.

**Reason (R):** Under this method the rate is applied to the original cost of the asset every year.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true, because the book value is highest in the first year. The reason is false: the rate is applied to the opening book value, not to the original cost, which is what makes the charge fall.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Freehold land owned by Yamini Estates, an imagined firm, is usually not depreciated.

**Reason (R):** Land is a fixed asset of the business.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Many fixed assets, such as machines, are depreciated, so being a fixed asset is not why land is left out. Land is usually not depreciated because it does not wear out and its useful life is unlimited.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Creating a provision for repairs reduces the profit shown by Zarina Garages, an imagined firm, whereas creating a general reserve does not reduce the profit earned.

**Reason (R):** A provision is charged against profit, while a general reserve is set aside out of the profit that has already been found.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A secret reserve is shown on the liabilities side of the balance sheet under the heading of reserves.

**Reason (R):** A secret reserve may be created by undervaluing the assets of the business.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The assertion is false, because a secret reserve is not disclosed in the balance sheet at all. The reason is true, since undervaluing assets is one way of building such a reserve, but it supports the idea of concealment rather than the assertion.

questions.stem_md: True or false: the depreciation charged for a year is an expense that is paid out in cash during that year.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Depreciation is a non-cash expense: the cost of the asset was paid when it was bought, and the yearly charge only allocates part of that cost to the year.

questions.stem_md: True or false: when a Provision for Depreciation A/c is kept, the machinery account of an imagined firm continues to show the machines at their original cost.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The depreciation is credited to the provision account, so the machinery account is not reduced and stays at cost until an asset is sold.

questions.stem_md: True or false: an imagined firm that has made a loss for the year can create a general reserve out of that year's profit.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A reserve is an appropriation of profit, so it needs profit to be set aside from. A year with a loss has no profit to appropriate, and a provision, unlike a reserve, may still be charged.

questions.stem_md: Under the straight line method, yearly depreciation = (cost − ___) ÷ ___ of the asset.

questions.stem_md: Define depreciation and state one feature of it.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and one feature.

answer.model_answer_md: **Depreciation** is the decline in the value of a fixed asset through use, passage of time or obsolescence, charged by spreading its depreciable cost over its useful life. It is a **non-cash expense** charged against the revenue of each year.

marking_scheme.step: Definition: fall in the value of a fixed asset, cost spread over life
One feature, for example non-cash expense

questions.stem_md: State two causes of depreciation, giving one example of each from the books of Ajay Cycles, an imagined firm.
questions.solution_md: Two causes with an example each.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **Wear and tear:** the welding machines of Ajay Cycles lose efficiency through daily use. (b) **Obsolescence:** a cutting machine is replaced because a newer, faster model is available even though it still works.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why Bhoomi Traders, an imagined firm, must charge depreciation every year even though no cash is paid out.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons from matching, true profit, true financial position, replacement and tax.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **Matching:** the cost of an asset helps earn revenue over several years, so a part of it must be charged against each year's revenue. (b) **True profit and position:** without it, profit is overstated and the asset is shown at more than it is worth.

questions.stem_md: State one merit and one limitation of the straight line method of depreciation.
questions.solution_md: One advantage and one drawback.

answer.model_answer_md: **Merit:** it is simple to understand and apply, and the charge is the same each year. **Limitation:** the charge stays equal even though repairs rise in later years, so the total burden on profit is uneven.

questions.stem_md: State one merit and one limitation of the written down value method of depreciation.
questions.solution_md: One advantage and one drawback.

answer.model_answer_md: **Merit:** the heavy charge in the early years is offset by lower repairs, and the later fall in depreciation is offset by rising repairs, so the total burden is more even. **Limitation:** the book value never falls to nil, and the calculation is harder.

questions.stem_md: Name the two ways of recording depreciation in the books and state how the asset appears in the balance sheet under each.
questions.solution_md: The direct way and the provision way.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **Charging depreciation to the asset account:** the asset is shown at cost less depreciation to date, that is, at book value. (b) **Creating a provision for depreciation account:** the asset is shown at original cost, with the provision deducted from it.

marking_scheme.step: Direct charge: shown at book value
Provision account: cost shown, provision deducted

questions.stem_md: What is an Asset Disposal A/c? When does Chetna Mills, an imagined firm, open it?
questions.solution_md: A temporary account to find the result of a sale, used under the provision method.

answer.model_answer_md: An **Asset Disposal A/c** is a temporary account in which the cost, the accumulated depreciation and the sale proceeds of an asset are brought together to find the profit or loss on its sale. It is opened when an asset is sold and a provision for depreciation account is kept.

marking_scheme.step: Purpose: to find profit or loss on sale
Used when a provision account is kept and an asset is sold

questions.stem_md: What is a provision? Give one example.
questions.solution_md: A charge against profit for a known liability or loss.

answer.model_answer_md: A **provision** is an amount charged against profit for a known liability or a likely loss whose exact amount is not certain. **Example:** a provision for doubtful debts, or a provision for taxation.

marking_scheme.step: Charge against profit for a known liability or loss of uncertain amount

questions.stem_md: What is a secret reserve? State one way in which Dilip Spices, an imagined firm, could create one.
questions.solution_md: A reserve hidden from the balance sheet, built by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities.

answer.model_answer_md: A **secret reserve** is a reserve that is not shown in the balance sheet, so outsiders cannot know of it. It can be created by undervaluing assets, for example by showing the stock below its true value, or by overvaluing liabilities.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning: not disclosed in the balance sheet

questions.stem_md: State two reasons why reserves are important to a business such as Esha Handlooms, an imagined firm.
questions.solution_md: Any two of strengthening, meeting losses, expansion and even payouts.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Reserves **strengthen the financial position** of the business and help it meet unexpected losses without borrowing. (b) Reserves provide funds for **expansion**, and for evening out payouts to the owners in lean years.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between provisions and reserves on five points.
questions.solution_md: Nature, effect on profit, presentation, purpose and compulsion.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Provision | Reserve |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Charge against profit for a known liability or loss | Appropriation, a part of profit kept back |
| Effect on profit | Reduces the profit | Does not reduce the profit earned |
| Presentation | Deducted from an asset or shown among liabilities | Shown with the owners' funds |
| Purpose | To meet a known liability or loss | To strengthen the business |
| Compulsion | Made even if there is no profit | Created only out of profit, by choice |

questions.stem_md: Explain the causes of depreciation and the need for charging it.
questions.solution_md: Four causes and the reasons for charging it every year.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Causes:** (1) wear and tear through use; (2) expiry of legal rights such as a lease or patent; (3) obsolescence, when newer technology makes an asset out of date; (4) abnormal factors such as accidents or fire.

**Need:** (1) matching, so that each year bears the cost of the asset that helped earn its revenue; (2) true profit, since ignoring it overstates profit; (3) true financial position, so the asset is not shown at more than its worth; (4) funds for replacement, as profit not withdrawn stays in the business; (5) tax and legal needs.
